vignette:
Daniel Weber had been living alone in a small apartment in a Chicago high-rise for nearly a year when he finally agreed to come in for help. At 37, he carried himself with the controlled precision of someone used to spreadsheets, deadlines, and clean forecasts, but he said his evenings had become dominated by a different kind of accounting: checking the locks twice, listening for sounds in the hallway, and trying to decide whether the quiet meant safety or danger. He and his ex-wife had divorced eight months earlier, and he described the breakup as another layer of distance he had not had the energy to explain. He worked as a financial analyst, a job that kept him in front of screens for long hours, but even there he found himself scanning for exits, noticing who came and went from the office, and feeling most unsettled when the floor became unusually quiet.

Daniel traced the beginning of the problem back to a captivity experience several years earlier, when he had been taken and held against his will in a frightening, prolonged ordeal that stripped him of any control over where he went, when he slept, or what happened next. He did not go into every detail at once, but what he did describe was enough to make clear how powerless he had felt: the uncertainty, the waiting, the sense that he was being handled rather than treated as a person. In the weeks after, certain sensations remained unusually close to the surface. He said that when he tried to remember the event, he could sometimes smell the same odors that were present then, and that the memory did not feel distant or faded the way ordinary memories did. Instead, it came back with a clarity that startled him, as if he were seeing it again in exact detail rather than recalling it from years away. He could still picture particular moments with sharpness, and the vividness of those memories made them feel "more real than normal," as he put it, which was part of why he avoided giving them much room.

He noticed that complete silence could be as unsettling as a sudden noise. In his apartment, if the building went quiet at night, he found himself alert immediately, listening for what might come next. He would stay awake longer than he wanted to, not because he felt rested by waiting but because he felt he needed to remain watchful in order to be prepared. Falling asleep became difficult for the same reason; he described lying in bed with his body tense, as though sleep meant losing the one advantage he had. He had also become guarded inside his own home, checking windows and the deadbolt after coming in from work and feeling uneasy if he could not account for every sound in the apartment.

Certain social moments brought the event into the present in ways he found hard to explain to other people. He had noticed that the sound of children crying could hit him abruptly and make his whole body tighten. It happened once in the lobby of his building when a child began to cry near the elevators; Daniel felt flooded by the noise, stood still for a moment, and then took the stairs instead of waiting. Physical affection affected him too. Hugs, even brief ones from family members or friends, left him uncomfortable and stiff, and he often found reasons to step back or keep interactions short. He was embarrassed by that reaction because it felt at odds with who he thought he was, especially since he had once been easygoing and warm in close relationships. Now he experienced many of those moments as reminders that his body had become difficult to trust.

Over time, Daniel also found himself turning over the moral meaning of what had happened to him. What troubled him most was not only the event itself but what he believed he had been forced to do in order to survive it. He said he had acted in ways that went against who he was, and that this left him with a persistent sense of shame that did not lessen when he tried to reason with it. He described feeling like an object during captivity, not like a person, and the phrase came out with visible discomfort, as if it captured something he had long struggled to put into words. He was also angry in a way that remained unresolved because the people responsible had faced no consequences. That fact stayed with him, and he returned to it repeatedly, with a flatness that suggested how long he had been carrying it.

At work, Daniel had managed to keep functioning, but only by narrowing his life. He declined invitations that involved close contact or crowded settings, and his divorce had made the apartment quieter, which in practice meant more time alone with his vigilance. Friends had noticed that he seemed jumpy and harder to reach, but he had mostly kept the details to himself. What finally brought him in was the combination of worsening sleep, the strain of always being on guard, and a recent episode in which a child crying in a neighboring apartment and the sudden silence that followed left him so shaken that he sat in his car outside his building for several minutes before he could go upstairs. He came to treatment hoping to sleep without feeling he had to stay alert and hoping, in a way that sounded almost hesitant, to feel like a person again rather than someone still waiting for the danger to return.
